replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's something that surprises most people: an LLM never sees your words.

Before anything else happens, your text gets chopped into pieces called **tokens**, and each token is swapped for a number. GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 of these pieces.

[EX]Imagine the sentence "I put cash in the bank" gets split into tokens like "I", " put", " cash", " in", " the", " bank", and each piece is replaced by an ID number. (The numbers would be made up here, since every tokenizer uses different ones.)[/EX]

Notice that "bank" gets the same token whether you mean a money bank or a river bank. The model sorts out the meaning later, by looking at the neighboring tokens.

[KEY]An LLM doesn't read words; it works on numbers that stand in for chunks of text.[/KEY]

[Q]
Why does the word "bank" get the same token in "cash in the bank" and "bank of the river"?
A) Tokenization just converts text pieces to numbers
B) The model has already decided which meaning is correct
C) The model looks up each sentence in a database
ANS: A
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked A) Tokenization just converts text pieces to numbers
replies.raw:
Exactly. Tokenization is just a conversion step, and it has no idea what the text means. The meaning gets worked out afterward.

Which brings us to the main job of an LLM: **next-token prediction**. After turning your prompt into tokens, the model does one thing, over and over. It calculates how likely every token in its vocabulary is to come next, picks one, adds it to the text, and repeats.

[EX]Take "The cat sat on the ___". Nearly all the probability lands on a few tokens like " mat", " floor", or " couch", so the model is very confident. Now take "My favorite thing to do on a weekend is ___". Thousands of continuations fit, so the probability is spread thin and no single token dominates.[/EX]

This is also why an LLM isn't a search engine. It doesn't look up an answer anywhere. It builds one token at a time from learned patterns about what tends to follow what.

[KEY]An LLM writes by repeatedly predicting the most plausible next token, and its confidence depends on how many continuations fit.[/KEY]

[Q]
In "The capital of France is ___", how would the model's next-token prediction look?
A) Probability is spread evenly across thousands of tokens
B) One token, " Paris", gets nearly all the probability
C) The model searches the web for the answer first
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked C) The model searches the web for the answer first
replies.raw:
Not quite. This is the "looks up answers like a search engine" idea, and it's the most common mistake here.

Some chatbots can search the web as an added feature, but that's not what next-token prediction is. The prediction step itself never searches anything. During training, the model saw "The capital of France is Paris" in many forms, so the pattern "capital of France is" is almost always followed by " Paris".

That pattern is baked into its numbers, which is why nearly all the probability piles onto one token.

The difference from my earlier example: "The cat sat on the ___" had a few good options, while this one has essentially one. A near-certain answer comes from a pattern seen over and over, not from a lookup.

[KEY]When an LLM seems to "know" a fact, it's usually because one continuation is overwhelmingly likely, not because it retrieved anything.[/KEY]

Let's try it again with a fresh case.

[Q]
For "Roses are red, violets are ___", what would the model's prediction most likely look like?
A) Probability is spread evenly across thousands of tokens
B) The model searches for the poem online first
C) One token, " blue", gets nearly all the probability
ANS: C
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked C) One token, " blue", gets nearly all the probability
replies.raw:
Right, and notice why. The rhyme is so well known that one token dominates, with no lookup involved.

Now let's put this to work. Here's your exercise.

Below are three sentences, each ending in a blank where the model must predict the next token:

1. "Two plus two equals ___"
2. "After school, I want to ___"
3. "Happy birthday to ___"

For each one:
- Say whether the model's confidence in its top choice would be **HIGH** or **LOW**.
- Explain why, in your own words, using what we covered about how many continuations fit.

Answer all three, and give your reasoning for each, not just the label.

replies.user: For the exercise, concretely: the model is most confident at the end of a strong collocation — the slot where one continuation dominates training text. It's least confident at an open slot where several continuations are all plausible. Strong learned pattern → high confidence; open choice → low confidence.
replies.raw:
Your general principle is right: a strong learned pattern means one continuation dominates (HIGH), and an open slot with many plausible options means LOW. That's the core idea of the lesson.

But the exercise asked for something specific: a verdict on each of the three sentences, with your reasoning for each. You've given the rule without applying it, so I can't tell yet whether you can use it on real examples.

Try it on each one, in your own words:

2. "After school, I want to ___"

For each, say HIGH or LOW, and name what makes the continuation either dominant or wide open.

replies.user: Naming the exact spots: high confidence — the final word of your sentence, because the phrase leading into it is a fixed expression. Low confidence — immediately after the first word, because almost any word class could follow there.

Here's something that surprises most people: an LLM never sees your words. It only sees numbers.

Before your prompt reaches the model, it gets chopped into pieces called **tokens**, and each piece is swapped for a number. GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 of these pieces.

[KEY]An LLM doesn't read words; it reads a sequence of token numbers.[/KEY]

[EX]Imagine the sentence "I put cash in the bank" gets split into tokens and turned into numbers like 40, 3013, 8515, 304, 279, 6201 (made-up numbers, just for illustration). The model works only with that list of numbers.[/EX]

Here's a twist: the word "bank" gets the same token whether it means money or a riverbank.

[Q]
Why does a model's input end up as numbers instead of words?
A) Numbers let the model look up the answer in a database
B) Numbers are how the model remembers the training data word for word
C) Numbers are what the model's math can actually process
ANS: C
[/Q]

Yes, low confidence is right, and your reasoning is exactly the point. Many tokens fit the slot ("essay", "answers", "work", "presentation"), so the probability spreads across all of them instead of piling onto one. No single token dominates.

You also got the first blank right: "studied all night" narrows things down to a small cluster like "exam" or "test", so the top token stands out.

That's how next-token prediction works: attention reads the context, then the model scores every token in its vocabulary, and confidence depends on whether the scores concentrate or spread out.
